summary: Defines a YANG data model that describes microwave and millimeter-wave radio links within a network topology. It lets management systems represent these wireless links alongside other network connections.

eli5.summary: Some network connections are radio beams between towers instead of cables. This gives a standard way to draw those beams on a map of the network that software can read.

subtitle: A YANG model for describing microwave and millimeter-wave radio links and their carriers inside a network topology.

tldr.problem: Management systems need a standard way to represent microwave radio links, with their carriers, alongside the higher-layer links such as Ethernet that run over them.
tldr.mechanism: A YANG module, ietf-microwave-topology, augments the TE Topologies model (RFC 8795), itself based on the Network Topologies model (RFC 8345). It adds microwave nodes, termination points, radio links, carriers and bandwidth.
tldr.outcome: A controller can see how a radio link's status or capacity affects the links above it and can use that information for path computation and radio optimization.

today: RFC 9656 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2024, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Describing Microwave Links in a Topology
sections.content:
This document defines a YANG data model to describe microwave and millimeter-wave radio links in a network topology. The text uses the word microwave for both. The model covers radio links, the supporting carriers, and the associated carrier termination points from RFC 8561.

A carrier is a single link providing transport capacity over the air, typically defined by its transmitting and receiving frequencies. A radio link provides the combined capacity of its carriers in aggregated or protected configurations. That capacity carries traffic for higher layers such as Ethernet and Time-Division Multiplexing (TDM).

The model augments the TE Topologies model in RFC 8795, which is based on the Network Topologies model in RFC 8345.
sections.eli5: A radio link is like a team of walkie-talkie channels between two towers. Each channel is a carrier, and the team together carries the traffic.

sections.title: Layers and Use Cases
sections.content:
Microwave point-to-point radio provides Layer 0 or Layer 1 connectivity between two termination points. It cannot cross-connect or switch traffic across several radio links. Instead a payload from a higher layer, normally Layer 2 Ethernet, rides over the link. Switching happens at that higher layer, where the radio link ends.

The model is expected to be used between a Provisioning Network Controller (PNC) and a Multi-Domain Service Coordinator (MDSC) from RFC 8453. The listed use cases are:

  • Correlating radio links with the higher-layer links they support, to see how a radio link's performance or status affects traffic above.
  • Passing characteristics such as bandwidth up to higher layers, where they can guide path selection for a connection or service.
  • Optimizing radio link configurations across a network to minimize interference and maximize overall capacity.
sections.eli5: The radio beam only carries parcels between two towers. The towers then hand the parcels to the road network above. Knowing how healthy the beam is helps choose good roads.

sections.title: The Module Structure
sections.content:
The module ietf-microwave-topology (prefix mwt) adds several containers to the TE topology model. Each is a presence container, and each augmentation applies only when the network is marked with the microwave topology type.

  • mw-topology marks a network as a microwave topology.
  • mw-node marks a node as a microwave node.
  • mw-tp marks a termination point, as either a radio link termination point (microwave-rltp) or a carrier termination point (microwave-ctp).
  • mw-link marks a link, as either a microwave-radio-link or a microwave-carrier.
  • mw-bandwidth is a read-only nominal bandwidth in bits per second added under the maximum link bandwidth.

A radio link has an rlt-mode container with num-bonded-carriers and num-protecting-carriers, both uint32. A carrier has tx-frequency and channel-separation (both in kHz and writable), and read-only actual-rx-frequency, actual-tx-cm (actual coding and modulation), actual-snir in dB and actual-transmitted-level in dBm. Many of these relate to data nodes of the same name in RFC 8561.
sections.eli5: The model gives tags for towers, antennas, radio beams and single channels. A beam tag says how many channels work together and how many are spares. A channel tag says its frequency and how strong its signal is.

sections.title: Radio Links, Carriers and Client Layers
sections.content:
A microwave radio link is always an aggregate of one or more carriers in various configurations or modes. The supporting carriers are identified by their termination points and listed as bundled links in the te-link-config of the radio link. The exact mix is given by rlt-mode, with modes such as 1+0, 2+0 and 1+1.

A radio link normally carries Layer 2 Ethernet. The standard supporting-network, supporting-node, supporting-link and supporting-termination-point leafs from RFC 8345 are expected to link a higher-layer topology to the microwave layer beneath it.

Because microwave is point-to-point, many TE topology leafs do not apply. The admin-status and oper-status leafs apply only to carriers, not to radio links, since radio links are enabled or disabled through their carriers.
sections.eli5: A radio link is a bundle of channels. The Ethernet network above is drawn as sitting on top of that bundle, and the model records which one rests on which.

sections.title: Worked Examples in the Appendices
sections.content:
The appendices show the model in JSON instance data for small networks, with an L2 Ethernet network over a microwave network. Two bonded-versus-protected cases are given.

In the 2+0 example, num-bonded-carriers is 2 and num-protecting-carriers is 0. Both carriers are active, so there is no redundancy and there is more capacity. In the 1+1 example, num-bonded-carriers is 1 and num-protecting-carriers is 1, so a standby carrier protects the active one.

Appendix B is non-normative. It shows how the model combines with the interface reference topology and bandwidth-availability-topology models, which are Internet-Drafts, and gives a JSON snippet for geolocation information.
sections.eli5: With two active channels you go faster but have no backup. With one active and one spare, you go slower but have a backup if the first fails.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The module defines data that is meant to be accessed through NETCONF (RFC 6241) or RESTCONF (RFC 8040). The mandatory-to-implement secure transport is SSH for NETCONF (RFC 6242) and TLS for RESTCONF (RFC 8446). The NETCONF access control model (RFC 8341) can limit which users reach which operations and content. The security considerations of RFC 8345 also apply.

Writable data nodes can be sensitive if modified without protection. The RFC names two cases:

  • rlt-mode: a malicious client could change how the radio link is configured and so change its intended behavior.
  • tx-frequency and channel-separation: a malicious client could change a carrier's frequency setup, which could alter its behavior or make the configuration invalid and stop its operation.
sections.eli5: Only trusted people should be allowed to change the radio settings. Someone who changed the channel setup could knock the link off the air.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA assigned a new XML namespace URI, urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-microwave-topology, in the IETF XML Registry, with the IESG as registrant. It also recorded the module in the YANG Module Names registry as ietf-microwave-topology, with prefix mwt and reference RFC 9656. The module is not maintained by IANA.
sections.eli5: The module was given an official name and address in the public lists so nobody else uses the same ones.
